<reason>PRO built a coherent case (upstream cause, coverage travels with pricing conditions, brand-level exclusion as the real lever) and progressively narrowed the clash to risk allocation and the diabetes/obesity distinction. CON's leverage argument was its genuine spine and it pressed a real mechanical worry—once coverage is mandated, the indication-level walk-away disappears and outcomes language may be hollow. But under pressure CON's answers were weaker: it never named an instance where fragmented refusal beat pooled negotiation (a dodge on PRO's Q2), and its A1 reduced the diabetes/obesity distinction to "scale," which PRO exploited effectively in closing. CON also conceded plans already move net prices by preferring one GLP-1 over another, which supports PRO's brand-level lever. PRO answered CON's pressure questions directly with a plausible mechanism (class coverage, competitor substitution, negotiation authority) and used approximate, plausible background facts without fake precision. PRO's two clipped turns are a minor execution cost. CON was disciplined and stayed on mechanism, but its closing largely restated rather than resolved the clash. Clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The leverage exchange: CON [B1.5]/[B2.5] argued a mandate surrenders the buyer's hard no; PRO [A2.2]/[A4.3] countered that insurers have exercised that no for years without moving prices because it is aimed at the patient, not the seller, and that brand-level exclusion is the only no that has ever moved a manufacturer. CON's reply that brand-swapping isn't an indication-level walk-away was real but undercut by its own concession that plans already shift net prices by preferring one GLP-1 over another.</best_rebuttal>
